title: A quick mid-summer update from the vineyards of Champagne
summary:
Like many wine regions around the world, Champagne has now moved into a sustained stretch of heat and drought conditions, with three heatwaves already this season and another likely on the way this week. Spring was cool, with some frost pressure that reduced yields, though not in a way that appears to have been detrimental to overall quality. An early harvest in mid-August had been widely expected. However, the combination of heat and a prolonged lack of rainfall has slowed things considerably, with vines effectively in survival mode and ripening stalling in many places. Veraison is in the early stages, but more slowly than expected, even over the past couple of weeks here on the ground. The vineyards themselves look in good shape. Canopies are healthy, disease pressure has been low, and while there have been a few quiet mentions of oidium, it doesn’t seem to be a major concern. There is some sunburn showing after repeated heat events, but so far it looks relatively limited and easy to manage. The main question now is berry size. Clusters are generally loose, with small berries, and rain is needed to bolster juice levels. Growers are hoping for timely rainfall to help restart ripening and allow the berries, including the smaller “hens and chicks,” to fill out. Without that, the harvest may not end up quite as early as initially expected, despite the head start to the season. With veraison still moving slowly, many growers are taking a brief pause before harvest... Read More

title: R.H. Drexel: Along the High Embankments: Deepening the Wine Culture of Santa Barbara Wine Country
summary:
“I wanted to see…a lot of my painting deal with the ocean, the sky, the horizon, and environmental policy, and why not take that into the physical realm and address the subjects literally through staring at the horizon, exposing works to the saltwater and rain, feeling the motion of a ship, dealing with sea sickness. I’m curious if they remain calm or perhaps, they turn a different direction and get a little more chaotic themselves, searching for what feels more like home.” Cole Sternberg                        the nature of breathing in salt                        A predictable Pacific chill has descended upon the Santa Maria Valley this blustery June evening as I make my way inside a large Brutalist-like concrete bunker just off East Clark Avenue, not far from California highway 101. A once-abandoned underground barrel room, this imposing structure is the new home of Presqu’ile x LAND, a visionary, sweeping artistic collaboration between the Murphy family of Santa Maria Valley and the Los Angeles Nomadic Division.  The fresh partnership signals a deepening of wine culture, not only for this sub-appellation, but for all of Santa Barbara County. The culture of a winegrowing region isn’t just about the wines born and raised there, or the wineries and vineyards that populate its landscape, for that matter, or even the often-big personalities who lead the charge in building its reputation. title: Jeb Dunnuck: Up From The Cellar 30
summary:
This latest Up From The Cellar is another eclectic mix! First and foremost, it includes a number of Northern Rhônes that I missed getting into the regional report earlier this year (full report). Producers included here are François Villard, Yves Cuilleron, Christophe Pichon, and Clusel-Roch. A heartfelt apology for missing those wines earlier. Beyond that, we have a number of new releases from California, as well as the full list of 2024s from Carter. There’s a small retrospective from Quintessa as well. The report is heavy on older Bordeaux, with some real gems that I was thrilled to taste. There are some First Growths from legendary years, as well as a mix of other terrific châteaux with some real age. This report includes the latest releases from Château de la Négly. These will fall to my colleague Andy Chabot going forward, but I was thrilled to be able to taste them. The lineup is packed with rich, textured, yet beautifully balanced wines. I also was able to sit down with Antoine Veiry of Château Montus and certainly came away impressed. The whites are brilliant as well as ageworthy, and I think the reds here bring lots of power and structure, with the newer releases showing another level of elegance. These are terrific wines. There’s also a handful of Burgundies. I purchased a set of the 2019s from Domaine Rossignol-Trapet and the wines showed beautifully. And last but not least, there are a handful of beautiful Southern Rhônes. As always, I... Read More

title: Importer Highlight: Hand Picked Selections
summary:
My ongoing coverage of the small, artisanal importers continues with this latest report on Hand Picked Selections, now under the ownership of Sunil Khanna and business partner Chris Desor. Sunil worked alongside founder Dan Kravitz for some 14 years before taking the reins, and the portfolio remains exactly what longtime followers have come to expect: a deep well of family-owned growers, small estates, and top co-ops sourced from across Europe and beyond. This latest tasting confirms the quality and value are very much intact, with a wide range of wines spanning the Languedoc, Roussillon, Savoie, Burgundy, Chablis, Sancerre, and Provence, with a mix of terrific summer quaffers as well as serious wines for the cellar. These wines were tasted at my office in Colorado, and as always with this portfolio, there’s plenty here to satisfy both the palate and the pocketbook.
